title: Tenant slicing and privacy fallback — design notes
body:
Purpose and scope:
This note captures an approach for Tenant Slicing + Privacy Fallback for a mid-market retail POC that must: (a) host multiple tenant workloads with varying data residency requirements, (b) guarantee privacy separation for a subset of tenants, and (c) provide graceful fallback to lower-cost/shared capacity during peaks without violating SLOs or data controls.

Customer context (summary):
- Retailer group running a conversational product for store associates and supply planners.
- 6 initial tenants in scope: 3 US-only, 2 EU-only (data residency needs), 1 highly-regulated pilot (on-prem preference).
- Expected peak qps: 600 requests/min across all tenants; typical p99 latency SLO: 300ms generation tail for short prompts.
- Budget: constrained on Hosted costs; customer wants a migration path from Hosted -> Dedicated slices or Private for critical tenant.

Design goals (ranked):
1) Privacy and compliance isolation for EU + regulated tenant.
2) Predictable latency for high-priority tenant (p99 <= 300ms).
3) Cost efficiency (use shared capacity where safe).
4) Minimal operational complexity for POC timeframe (12 weeks).
5) Clear rollback paths and observability per-tenant.

Constraints and non-goals:
- Non-goal: Full production-grade autoscaling policies — POC uses conservative manual scaling knobs.
- Constraint: No HSM/KMS on customer side for POC; encryption-at-rest handled by Redwood-managed KMS.
- Constraint: Networking to customer VPC can take 6+ weeks — design must allow parallel progress with Hosted variants.

Proposed architecture options (three variants) — tradeoffs below each: 
1) Hosted-first tenant-slice with regional isolation (fastest to deliver)
  - Overview: All tenants on Redwood Hosted region pools; routing by tenant->region mapping. EU tenants routed to EU region pool with controls to prevent cross-region cache leakage. Regulated tenant pinned to EU pool with stricter logging retention.
  - Privacy controls: Per-tenant prefixes hashed before caching; strict keying to prevent cross-tenant KV reuse. Audit logs retained to customer retention policy.
  - Fallback: When EU pool saturated, traffic can failover to a compatible model on US pool but only for non-sensitive endpoints (explicit allow-list). Fallback requires tenant opt-in; regulated tenant default = no fallback.
  - Pros: Fastest to demo; lowest operational lift; centralized observability.
  - Cons: Residual trust required (Hosted KMS), limited absolute isolation, potential cold-start tail impact on large bursts.

2) Dedicated-tenant-slices (mid-term, cost predictable)
  - Overview: Reserve Dedicated capacity (GPU pool per 2 tenants) with tenant placement policies: high-priority tenants get pinned slices, smaller tenants share a pooled slice.
  - Privacy controls: Dedicated pools deployed in customer-approved regions; strict network ACLs; per-tenant model pinning and token-level access controls.
  - Fallback: When Dedicated pool approaches capacity, route overflow to Hosted scratch pool with per-request redaction and synthetic-data toggles. Overflow uses rate-limited mechanical shims (queue + reject thresholds) to preserve p99.
  - Pros: Stronger isolation, predictable costs via reserved capacity, easier SLA mapping.
  - Cons: Higher committed cost; longer lead time to provision GPUs for POC (2–4 weeks).

3) Private hybrid (on-prem for regulated tenant + hosted for others)
  - Overview: Private deployment placed for regulated tenant in their data center / VPC (or our on-prem appliance). Other tenants use Hosted or Dedicated depending on load.
  - Privacy controls: Regulated tenant has full data residency, local KMS/HSM integration (if customer requests in later phase), and full trace isolation.
  - Fallback: Local private instance provides primary; fallback to Dedicated within same jurisdiction (EU Dedicated) using encrypted transit and strict telemetry suppression. Failover requires active network peering and pre-authorized keys.
  - Pros: Highest privacy guarantee for the regulated tenant; satisfies strict compliance.
  - Cons: Most complex operationally; longer timeline and coordinate with customer infra team for networking.

Routing and policy matrix (implementation notes):
- Routing decisions based on: tenant metadata (residency flag), endpoint sensitivity (sensitive vs non-sensitive), current pool load.
- Policy examples:
  - If tenant.residency==EU and endpoint.sensitivity==high -> route to EU Dedicated or Private only.
  - If pool.load>85% -> initiate queued shed algorithm: (1) degrade streaming to non-streaming for low priority tenants, (2) redirect non-sensitive to cheaper model family, (3) if still over threshold, rate-limit/503 for lowest priority group.
- Observability: tag traces and cost by tenant_id, route decision layer must emit "route.reason" metric and allow retrospective replay in evaluation harness.

KV / cache design considerations to avoid leakage:
- Strict key namespace: tenant_id:route:prompthash:sequence -> ensures no cross-tenant hits.
- Prefix caching disabled for EU-high-sensitivity tenants; fallback to per-request KV only if tenant consents.
- Cache warmers: pre-warm for high-priority tenant at rollout time; use small synthetic prompt sets.

Cost and capacity sketch (POC window 12 weeks):
- Assumptions: 600 rpspeak? Actually earlier said 600 requests/min = 10 rps peak. Use 10 rps*. Average tokens per request = 150 tokens. Token-rate implications: ~1500 tokens/sec -> ~5.4M tokens/hr.
- Hosted-first estimate (approx): $X/month (placeholder) — for POC we recommend using 2 r5-large equivalent pools with autoscaling off; expected cost ~ $6–8k for POC duration (12 weeks) including buffer.
- Dedicated slice estimate: Reserve a small GPU pool (2x A10-like instances) for high-priority tenants + 1 shared smaller instance for others -> expected commit ~$25k/month (higher, but gives predictable throughput).
- Private: Capex and ops variable; expect integration cost + 1–2 weeks infra effort and an onboarding execution cost ~ $10–15k one-time for POC.
- Action: Finance to convert placeholders to precise quotes once target model family and quantization profile decided.

Testing and rollout plan (12-week POC):
- Week 0–2: Confirm tenant classification, get sign-off on privacy flags, finalize model families and quantization targets.
- Week 2–4: Provision Hosted regional pools + implement routing layer. Wire up tenant tagging and per-tenant telemetry.
- Week 4–6: Run synthetic load tests (0.5x, 1x, 2x expected) and run privacy leak tests (prompt leakage corpus).
- Week 6–8: If Dedicated chosen, begin provisioning dedicated slices; if Private chosen for regulated tenant, start network peering and deployment.
- Week 8–10: Canary traffic for 1 high-priority tenant; monitor p99, cost, and error behaviors.
- Week 10–12: Full POC run, prepare decision brief and recommended next steps.

Risks and mitigations (quick):
- Risk: Cross-tenant KV/caching leakage -> Mitigation: aggressive namespace enforcement, caching disabled for flagged tenants.
- Risk: Unexpected peak causing SLO violations -> Mitigation: circuit breaker + pre-configured fallback routes and rate limiting.
- Risk: Networking delays for Private deployment -> Mitigation: run Hosted-first with toggle to attach private instance when network ready.

Open questions (need customer answers):
1) Acceptable fallback policy for each tenant (opt-in/opt-out)?
2) Does customer require customer-managed KMS for POC or is Redwood-managed KMS acceptable?
3) Which model families are acceptable for fallback (e.g., quantized Llama2 variants)?
4) Are there regulatory auditors who need log extracts? If so, what retention window?

Next steps (owners):
- Aisha: Draft customer decision brief + link to cost placeholders (due 2024-11-15).
- Tomás: Prototype routing service with tenant flagging + metric emission (proto by 2024-11-19).
- Priya: Coordinate with sales and legal on data residency checklist and draft DPA addendum for POC (due 2024-11-18).

Appendix (notes & references):
- Related internal playbooks: Tenant isolation checklist (Confluence), Dedicated cost modeling spreadsheet (link in linked_artifacts).
- Quick test scripts: /infra/tests/tenant-privacy-leak.sh (repo link in linked_artifacts).
- Decision heuristics we used: prioritize privacy > latency > cost for regulated tenant; prioritize latency > cost for commerce-facing tenant.

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep fallback conservative for demo; user-visible failure (503 with clear message) is better than silent non-compliant fallback.
- We should add a small eval harness to measure semantic quality delta when redirecting to cheaper model family (value for sales conversation).
- Post-POC: evaluate Dedicated commitment vs on-demand savings tradeoff.

-- end of notes --
